newsitem.title: KENYA: Group denounces Kenya justice, corrupt police.
newsitem.headline: Group denounces Kenya justice, corrupt police.

text.p: A human rights group said on Friday the destruction of a Nairobi shanty town demonstrated how Kenya's justice system has broken down and police were corrupt and violent.
In a report, London-based African Rights said the fate of Soweto shanty town in a Nairobi suburb was "a potent symbol of the human rights crisis in Kenya and the breakdown of law and order".
"Much of what is wrong with the political and justice system in Kenya is illuminated by the experiences of the residents of a shanty town called Soweto in Spring Valley, Nairobi," it said.
"In September 1996, Soweto was a multi-ethnic, thriving shanty township with some 6,000 residents occupying less than an acre of land," the human rights group said in a 22-page report.

"By January 1997, the site had been burnt down, turned into a wasteland, and ear-marked for lucrative development. Thousands were made homeless...there has been no official investigation into what happened."

African Rights said five years of rule by President Daniel arap Moi since multi-party polls in 1992 "have established a political culture that relies on corruption, manipulation and the use of force".
Moi, 73 and in power for 19 years, says he will stand for re-election in a general election later this year. Opposition parties are demanding deep political reforms before the polls.
"People have lost faith, and found fear, in institutions that are supposed to hold a decent and functioning society together," said African Rights, adding land rights in Kenya was a burning issue.

"Vital institutions, like the justice system and the police force, have collapsed to the extent that people resort to taking the law into their own hands," it added in a reference to what is known in Kenya as "mob justice" against suspected wrongdoers.
There was no immediate government reaction to the report.

It catalogued events at Soweto, named after the Johannesburg township, from a fire last October that virtually razed the shanty town to a continuing legal battle between former residents and a businessman and ruling party activist who owns the site.
It said the fire, which destroyed all but 35 of the 947 structures in Soweto, appeared to be an accident but opened the way for clearance of squatters, some of whom had lived there for 20 years.
The local district officer told residents after the fire Moi had given them a new plot of land on the other side of Nairobi and they should go there. But those who refused were attacked.

African Rights said thugs hired by the owner of the land demolished homes in Soweto and repeatedly clashed with residents, who as squatters under Kenyan law have rights to land where they have lived without dispute for 12 years or more.
It said police at first did nothing and then were bribed to guard gangs destroying houses until a demolition worker in a clash was beaten, stoned and then burned to death by squatters.
Police then beat and arrested residents until on January 30 a 200-strong demolition gang battled residents. Two gang members were killed but a wall and fence were erected around the site.

African Rights said some 4,000 former Soweto residents were dumped on the other side of Nairobi on an open, temporary site, which was previously used by animals on their way to a nearby slaughterhouse and had a burst sewage pipe running through it.
